summary.text: Set \(c=4n+2\) and \(e=2n+3\); Legendre’s formula and the inequality \(2\lfloor(c+e)/q\rfloor+\lfloor c/q\rfloor+\lfloor e/q\rfloor\le\lfloor3c/q\rfloor+\lfloor3e/q\rfloor\) compare every prime valuation, with the \(q=2,4\) terms supplying the two extra factors of \(2\). For \(p=3\), the valuation excess equals the base-3 digit sum of \(6n+5\), which is at least \(3\) because its first digit is \(2\) and the remaining positive quotient has digit sum at least \(1\); primes above \(3\) need no extra allowance, proving divisibility by \(2^2 3^3=108\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c=4n+2,\qquad e=2n+3,\qquad s=c+e=6n+5.
\]
Then
\[
3c=12n+6,\qquad 3e=6n+9.
\]
Thus the desired assertion is
\[
108\,c!\,e!\,(s!)^2\mid (3c)!(3e)!.
\]
We prove this by comparing the exponent of every prime on the two sides.

We first establish the floor inequality that controls the factorial ratio. For all positive integers \(q\) and all nonnegative integers \(c,e\),
\[
2\left\lfloor\frac{c+e}{q}\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac c q\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac e q\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{3c}{q}\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac{3e}{q}\right\rfloor. \tag{1}
\]
To prove this, write
\[
c=qC+r,
\qquad e=qE+t,
\qquad 0\le r,t<q.
\]
Removing the integral parts \(C,E\) from all the floors reduces (1) to
\[
2\left\lfloor\frac{r+t}{q}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{3r}{q}\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac{3t}{q}\right\rfloor. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, the terms involving \(C,E\) are \(3C+3E\) on both sides.

If \(r+t<q\), the left side of (2) is zero, so (2) is immediate. Otherwise,
\[
q\le r+t<2q,
\]
so its left side is \(2\). Put
\[
3r=qA+u,\qquad 3t=qB+v,
\qquad 0\le u,v<q.
\]
Because \(r+t\ge q\),
\[
q(A+B)+u+v=3(r+t)\ge 3q.
\]
But \(u+v<2q\), and consequently \(q(A+B)>q\). Hence \(A+B\ge2\), which is precisely (2). This proves (1).

For a prime \(p\), Legendre's formula gives
\[
v_p(m!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor, \tag{3}
\]
where only finitely many summands are nonzero. Formula (3) follows by counting, for every \(i\), the factors among \(1,2,\ldots,m\) which contribute at least \(i\) copies of \(p\); there are exactly \(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\) such factors.

Apply (1) with \(q=p^i\). For every \(i\ge1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac c{p^i}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac e{p^i}\right\rfloor
+2\left\lfloor\frac s{p^i}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{3c}{p^i}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac{3e}{p^i}\right\rfloor. \tag{4}
\]
Summing (4) and using Legendre's formula yields
\[
v_p(c!e!(s!)^2)\le v_p((3c)!(3e)!). \tag{5}
\]
This already handles all primes not dividing \(108\). It remains to prove that the excess valuation in (5) contains two additional factors of \(2\) and three additional factors of \(3\).

### The prime \(2\)

For \(p=2\), inequality (4) has an extra margin of at least one for each of \(i=1\) and \(i=2\).

For \(i=1\), direct evaluation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left\lfloor\frac c2\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac e2\right\rfloor
+2\left\lfloor\frac s2\right\rfloor\\
&=(2n+1)+(n+1)+2(3n+2)=9n+6,
\end{aligned}
\]
whereas
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3c}{2}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac{3e}{2}\right\rfloor
=(6n+3)+(3n+4)=9n+7.
\]
Thus the right side exceeds the left side by exactly one.

For \(i=2\), split according to the parity of \(n\). If \(n=2k\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lfloor\frac c4\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac e4\right\rfloor
+2\left\lfloor\frac s4\right\rfloor
&=2k+k+2(3k+1)=9k+2,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{3c}{4}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac{3e}{4}\right\rfloor
&=(6k+1)+(3k+2)=9k+3.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(n=2k+1\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lfloor\frac c4\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac e4\right\rfloor
+2\left\lfloor\frac s4\right\rfloor
&=(2k+1)+(k+1)+2(3k+2)=9k+6,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{3c}{4}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac{3e}{4}\right\rfloor
&=(6k+4)+(3k+3)=9k+7.
\end{aligned}
\]
Again the excess is exactly one. For every \(i\ge3\), ordinary inequality (4) supplies a nonnegative excess. Summing all these inequalities therefore gives
\[
v_2((3c)!(3e)!)-v_2(c!e!(s!)^2)\ge2. \tag{6}
\]
Since \(v_2(108)=2\), (6) supplies the entire required power of \(2\).

### The prime \(3\)

For the prime \(3\), it is more convenient to use the digit-sum form of Legendre's formula. Let \(S_3(x)\) denote the sum of the digits in the base-\(3\) expansion of \(x\). Then
\[
2v_3(x!)=x-S_3(x). \tag{7}
\]
To see this, write \(x=\sum_{j\ge0}a_j3^j\), with \(0\le a_j<3\). By (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
2v_3(x!)
&=2\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{x}{3^i}\right\rfloor
 =2\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{j\ge i}a_j3^{j-i}\\
&=\sum_{j\ge1}a_j(3^j-1)
 =x-\sum_{j\ge0}a_j
 =x-S_3(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplication by \(3\) merely appends a zero base-\(3\) digit, so
\[
S_3(3x)=S_3(x). \tag{8}
\]

Using (7), (8), and \(s=c+e\), calculate the valuation excess. We have
\[
\begin{aligned}
&2\Bigl(v_3((3c)!(3e)!)-v_3(c!e!(s!)^2)\Bigr)\\
&=\bigl(3c-S_3(3c)\bigr)+\bigl(3e-S_3(3e)\bigr)\\
&\quad-\bigl(c-S_3(c)\bigr)-\bigl(e-S_3(e)\bigr)
      -2\bigl(s-S_3(s)\bigr)\\
&=\bigl(3c+3e-c-e-2s\bigr)
  +\bigl(-S_3(c)-S_3(e)+S_3(c)+S_3(e)+2S_3(s)\bigr)\\
&=2S_3(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus in fact
\[
v_3((3c)!(3e)!)-v_3(c!e!(s!)^2)=S_3(s). \tag{9}
\]
Now
\[
s=6n+5=3(2n+1)+2.
\]
Accordingly, its least significant base-\(3\) digit is \(2\), and
\[
S_3(s)=2+S_3(2n+1).
\]
The integer \(2n+1\) is positive, so its base-\(3\) expansion contains at least one nonzero digit and therefore has digit sum at least \(1\). Hence
\[
S_3(s)\ge3.
\]
Together with (9), this gives
\[
v_3((3c)!(3e)!)-v_3(c!e!(s!)^2)\ge3. \tag{10}
\]
Since \(v_3(108)=3\), this supplies the required power of \(3\).

### Completion of the divisibility argument

The prime factorization of \(108\) is
\[
108=2^2\,3^3.
\]
For \(p=2\), inequality (6) says
\[
v_2(108c!e!(s!)^2)\le v_2((3c)!(3e)!).
\]
For \(p=3\), the same conclusion follows from (10). If \(p>3\) is prime, then \(p\nmid108\), so \(v_p(108)=0\), and the conclusion follows from (5). These are all primes.

All factorials involved are positive. By unique prime factorization, a positive integer divides another positive integer exactly when its exponent at every prime is no greater. Therefore
\[
108\,c!\,e!\,(s!)^2\mid(3c)!(3e)!.
\]
Substituting \(c=4n+2\), \(e=2n+3\), and \(s=6n+5\) gives
\[
108(4n+2)!(2n+3)!((6n+5)!)^2
\mid
(12n+6)!(6n+9)!.
\]
Consequently
\[
\frac{(12n+6)!(6n+9)!}
{108(4n+2)!(2n+3)!((6n+5)!)^2}
\]
is an integer for every nonnegative integer \(n\), as claimed.
